job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Carla Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Carla, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm at the kitchen table by eight, sending applications on my mother's old laptop while she's already out cleaning offices downtown. I share a bedroom with my sister Lena, who's sixteen, so I do the job hunting in the kitchen. I did electrical engineering in Gelsenkirchen, and I've sent about sixty applications since June and had three interviews. Afternoons I tutor a neighbour's boy in maths for twelve euros an hour, and that pays for my phone and bus pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because it means less panic. But I'd also say the bosses were never going to share the savings with us anyway. In my last internship at the municipal utility, the saved hours went into more targets for the same people, not shorter days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel nothing changes for me, and that's the problem. I'm top of my class, I owe about thirty-one thousand euros, and there are still three entry jobs within an hour's bus ride. A plateau means my search stays just as stuck as it is today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, maybe ten a week, and I'd ask my old professor Dr. Brandt to put me in touch with the substation firm he knows. I'd also keep tutoring and put every spare euro toward the loan. I wouldn't touch any AI tools, because I like knowing how my own work was done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Not scared of the technology, scared of the loan letters that come every month with my name on them. It feels like running up a down escalator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bosses wouldn't share the savings. Who do you mean, and what would you want from them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The managers who set the budgets, and the owners above them. I'd want them to hire two juniors for every retirement instead of leaving the seat empty. At the utility, two senior engineers retired in spring and nobody was hired, and I know because I was told to my face that the budget was frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mother on a night the fifth rejection arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Mum, it's not you, it's the numbers. She'd say, you'll find something, and then go to bed because she's up at five. I don't tell her how much the loan is, because she'd try to take extra shifts.

say: The **routine savings** are real but small, and employers will keep the profit.
I'd tell friends that **hiring freezes** are the real problem, not the technology.
think: I think my **search stays stuck** because few firms near me take graduates.
The **loan** is the thing keeping me awake, more than any machine.
do: Send about **ten applications** a week, including the substation firm Dr. Brandt knows.
Keep **tutoring** and put spare euros toward the loan.
Avoid AI tools and keep **doing things by hand**.
feel: **Tired** and stuck, with fear coming mostly from the monthly loan letters.
S0.quote: Two senior engineers retired in spring and nobody was hired, and I know because I was told to my face that the budget was frozen.
fieldNote: Her anger lands on **employers and budgets**, not on technology.
Shields her mother from the real **debt figure**.
Concrete and bitter about **unfilled retirements** at the utility where she interned.

steps.text: Send ten job applications a week, starting with the substation firm
Keep tutoring the neighbour's boy and pay down the loan
Carry on avoiding AI tools and doing calculations by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I feared: companies call it efficiency and call us lucky to apply. At the rail signalling firm where I interned, a lot of the checking of drawings was already being sent to software. I'd say the unions should be at the table now, not after the layoffs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think entry jobs are the first to go. The juniors check things, draft things and fill in test sheets, and that's exactly the list on the card. With few openings near me, one less graduate post means I'm out of the running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking at the state grid operator and the public rail company, because public employers hire slowly but they do hire. I'd join the engineers' union as a student member, which costs eight euros a month. I'd still not use the AI tools myself, although I know that sounds stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Angry too, because I did everything right, with top marks and two internships, and the ladder is losing its bottom rungs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd avoid the tools. Is that a plan, or a feeling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both, I suppose. I don't trust things I can't explain, and I can't explain how it reaches an answer. But I know a recruiter might see it as a gap, and I haven't solved that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost goes first if the search takes another year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bus pass, so I'd walk forty minutes to the tutoring jobs. Then the phone plan down to the cheapest. I'd never skip the loan payment, because the interest rate jumps if I do.

say: I'd say **efficiency** is a word companies use to avoid hiring juniors.
The unions should be **at the table** now, before layoffs start.
think: I think **entry-level checking** work is exactly what gets taken first.
Even **one fewer post** nearby could leave me out of the running.
do: Apply to the **grid operator** and public rail company, which hire slowly but steadily.
Join the engineers' union as a **student member** for eight euros a month.
Walk to tutoring jobs to **save the bus pass** if the search drags on.
feel: **Worried** and angry that top marks and two internships may not be enough.
S1.quote: I did everything right, with top marks and two internships, and the ladder is losing its bottom rungs.
fieldNote: Uses her **internship** at the rail firm as evidence for her fears.
Admits her **no-AI stance** may count against her, but hasn't resolved it.
Turns to **public employers and union** rather than to private firms.

steps.text: Apply to the state grid operator and the public rail company
Join the engineers' union as a student member
Drop the bus pass and walk to the tutoring jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments must act now, today, not in 2028. Tax the companies that benefit and fund a basic income. I'd say it loudly, at the union meeting and at the demonstration if one gets called.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree loses value in about two years, just as the loan reaches its worst. Electrical work has a hands-on side, which gives some extra time, but the design and calculation part I trained for goes first. I feel like I studied for a job that ends before it begins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get any job at all within six months, even a technician's post at the utility, because hands-on work gets the extra three years. I'd ask my mother and sister to help me plan the money, and I'd stop thinking about a master's. I'd also call the loan office to ask what happens if jobs vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. It's a feeling in my chest in the morning, that the thing I built my life around is being switched off. And I can't even point to a person to blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop thinking about a master's. What changed there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A master's is two more years and more debt for a market that may not exist when I finish. Before this, I thought it would set me apart. With two years of warning, it looks like paying to stand in a longer queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years change what you'd do compared with a longer warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means no experiments. I take the first safe thing, I stop trying to be picky about my field, and I treat the loan as the enemy. With longer I could study something else, but not with this little time.

say: Governments must **tax the winners** and fund a basic income before 2028.
I'd say it **loudly** at the union meeting and any demonstration.
think: My **degree loses value** just as the loan reaches its worst.
The **design and calculation** work I trained for goes first.
do: Take **any technician job** at the utility within six months, since hands-on work lasts longer.
Drop the **master's idea** to avoid more debt.
Call the **loan office** to ask what happens if jobs vanish.
feel: **Frightened**, with a chest-tight feeling that her chosen path is being switched off.
S2.quote: I feel like I studied for a job that ends before it begins.
fieldNote: Her **hands-on fallback** is concrete and reasoned.
Reverses her view on a **master's** because of the short window.
Anger has **no target** here, which seems to frighten her more.

steps.text: Apply for technician posts at the utility within six months
Call the loan office about repayment if jobs vanish
Speak at the union meeting about taxing AI winners
Write to my member of parliament about a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still say it's dangerous, but I'd say it more calmly. Five years is long enough to organise. I'd push for a retraining fund paid by the companies, with real wages during the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I get a first job, maybe two years of work, and then I'm in the same fix as everyone, but with some savings. The extra time means I can pay a good part of the loan. The fear is smaller but it's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any first job in the next year, learn the hands-on side of grid work, and put away three hundred euros a month if I can. I'd help Lena choose a course that isn't pure desk work. And I'd start going to local union meetings and bring two friends from my year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panicky than the two-year one, more like a long grey weather. It feels survivable if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena about her studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister Lena to look at jobs where someone must be there in person, like nursing, wiring, plumbing, rail track work. I would not tell her to follow me into pure design work. She'd roll her eyes, but she listens when it's about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do those extra three years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They give me a chance to be useful on site, where I'm needed, and to repay a big part of the loan before the thinking jobs go. Without them I'd be a graduate with nothing to stand on.

say: Five years is long enough to **organise** and demand a retraining fund.
Companies should pay for **real wages** during retraining courses.
think: I'll probably get **two years of work** before things turn.
Time lets me **pay down the loan**, which shrinks the fear.
do: Take **any first job** in the next year and learn grid work on site.
Save **three hundred euros** a month toward the loan.
Steer **Lena** toward courses that need people in person.
feel: Like **long grey weather**: not panic, but heavy and survivable if careful.
S3.quote: I'd tell my sister Lena to look at jobs where someone must be there in person, like nursing, wiring, plumbing, rail track work.
fieldNote: Mood eases but stays **anxious**, because she still has no offer.
Thinks as the **older sister**, with plans for Lena.
Uses the **robot delay** as a practical resource.

steps.text: Take the first technician job offered and learn grid work
Put three hundred euros a month toward the loan
Help Lena choose a hands-on course after school
Bring two classmates to the local union meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different conversation. I'd say it's a chance to build things properly, and that people who panic now are wasting the warning. I'd still say the rules need writing early, though, on who owns the benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine if I get a first job in the next year. A decade means I could clear the loan, build a real career and maybe move into the hands-on side of grid maintenance. The worry is more about whether the politicians will use the decade or waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a technician job first, get my professional licence, and go on a short course in the control systems side, which will outlast the design side. I'd save for a flat for me and Lena. I'd also join the union branch properly and maybe run for the young members' seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with an edge. It feels like having time, which most of this is about, and I don't often feel I have it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the politicians might waste the decade. What makes you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I watched the politicians with energy prices. They said they'd plan, then did nothing until the bills came. I'd rather the unions force the plan than wait for politicians to feel like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year picture, what do you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I take a licence, I go for a course, and I let myself aim at a good job rather than any job. In the two-year one I only survive. Here I can choose.

say: A decade is a **chance** to build things properly, if the rules get written early.
The question is **who owns the benefits**, and that must be settled soon.
think: If I land a first job soon, I'd probably be **fine**.
My real worry is whether **politicians use** the decade or waste it.
do: Get a **professional licence** and a short course in control systems.
Save for a **flat** for me and Lena.
Join the union branch and run for the **young members' seat**.
feel: **Hopeful with an edge**, because time is something she rarely feels she has.
S4.quote: I watched the politicians with energy prices. They said they'd plan, then did nothing until the bills came.
fieldNote: Only scenario where she lets herself **aim higher** than any job.
Mood lowest here because a **decade** buys loan repayment.

steps.text: Take a short course in control systems alongside the first job
Save for a small flat that Lena and I can share
Pay off the loan early using the technician's pay
Stand for the young members' seat in the union branch

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because there's no room to move. Money would help most: a pause on loan payments for graduates without work, and a public employer hiring juniors. Even a guaranteed apprenticeship at the grid operator would change my whole year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not lazy and I'm not behind. I did the work and the doors aren't opening, and the tools nobody asked me to use are part of why. I'd like someone to say that out loud to people my age.

headlineQuote: I'm not lazy and I'm not behind. I did the work and the doors aren't opening
portrait: Carla is a **top electrical engineering** graduate in a Ruhr town, still without an offer after sixty applications.
She carries about **31,000 euros** of debt and shares a bedroom with her sister Lena.
Her mother cleans offices, so there is **no family cushion**, and Carla tutors to cover her bus pass.
She blames **employers and frozen budgets**, trusts unions, and never uses AI tools.
Across the five worlds she leans on **public employers**, hands-on work and collective action, and her mood eases only with a decade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there is **no room** to adjust with the loan unpaid.
whatWouldHelp: A **pause** on graduate loan payments and a public employer that hires juniors.
A **guaranteed apprenticeship** at the grid operator.
